extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers in advertising/marketing and advertising practitioners (advertising managers, media planners), grant program stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for designing, conducting, and applying academic research on advertising (including lab and field methods, segmentation, message/source/channel factors, and applicability to practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audience-bound factors (race/national origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate advertising directed toward or involving Afro‑Americans and Mexican Americans; consider the audience-bound factor of race or national origin and the influence that this factor exerts in affecting response to advertising in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask respondents about general attitudes toward advertising, perception of specific types of advertising, and expectations regarding economic future; compare perceptions across racial groups to inform integrated consumer advertising decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider message-bound factors (messages tailored to racial groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the effects of advertising messages specifically designed to appeal to different racial groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research should examine how message content aimed at particular racial groups affects response, and whether messages reduce prejudice or influence behavior within targeted segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test reactions to integrated advertising (mixed-race depictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate reactions of black consumers (and other groups) to advertising depicting within the same ad both black and Caucasian models; relate such integrated advertising to overall sales and sales within racial segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although many practitioners cite social climate as rationale for integration, empirical investigation is needed to determine effects on different consumer segments and on sales outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid racial caricatures and stereotypes in portrayals
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid racial caricatures and stereotypes; portray Mexican‑Americans and other minorities in non-stereotypical ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray groups as purposeful and hard‑working in everyday life situations; inclusion is perceived as enhanced social recognition and progress and increases ad effectiveness according to respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for economic well-being as moderator of receptivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic well‑being and favorable future expectations moderate racial prejudice and receptivity to integrated advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those more optimistic about economic prospects are more favorably inclined toward advertising designed to reduce prejudice; measure respondents' expectations (home ownership, education, job advancement, travel, retirement) when studying prejudice-reduction ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segmentation within racial groups by motivational differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Market segmentation by race should not ignore motivational differences within a racial group (e.g., 'strivers' vs 'non-strivers').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment consumers by motivational orientations and economic aspirations as these predict differences in attitudes toward advertising and shopping behavior more precisely than race alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include source, channel, message, audience and their interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: A study of repetition (or other message effects) must take into account the combined effects of source, channels, message, and audience as well as interactions among them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not study message repetition in isolation; design experiments and models that include buyer segments, product types, brands, ad formats, colors, schedules, appeals, competitive activities, and media mixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validate laboratory techniques by transferability to field
rubrics_metrics.description: Laboratory techniques are useful only if results are transferable to real-world field situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare lab findings with field experiment outcomes (the grant compared eight lab studies with a large field experiment and found comparable results); only then can managers rely on lab methods for campaign prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize non-monotonic repetition effects (wearout and irritation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Too much repetition or exposure can produce a response curve that turns down due to boredom or irritation; the traditional monotonically rising learning-curve assumption is not always accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media scheduling should guard against excessive advertising weight; monitor for negative consumer reactions and adjust schedules accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for threshold and S-shaped response curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall repetition response curves can be S-shaped—rising slowly, then sharply, then leveling—implying a threshold number of exposures before effect is observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select media schedules according to campaign goals and the type of desired advertising response, because effectiveness of different schedules depends on the response being targeted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple measures matched to response types
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor responses using appropriate measures: physiological equipment for attention; recognition and recall tests for learning; attitude scales for attitudinal responses; simulated buying for overt behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different response types require different measurement tools; design studies that employ several complementary measures to capture the full range of effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study repetition effects across contextual variables
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying repetition and wearout, examine variation across buyer segments, product types, brands, ad formats or illustrations, colors, schedules, appeals, competitive activities, and media mixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include these factors in experimental design or modeling since they condition the shape and magnitude of repetition effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not uncritically generalize general communications models to advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising may possess unique properties that preclude direct transfer of general communications research and models to advertising contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether general communication findings hold for ads—people may accept favorable but logically invalid inferences from ads more readily than from news or letters; acceptance often reflects perceived advertiser intent rather than logical derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design: present identical content in different forms to test form effects
rubrics_metrics.description: To measure influence of message form, present identical content as ads, news stories, memos, or letters to different subjects and compare responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systematically varied forms with content held constant and include post-test measures of accuracy/derivation to detect differences in how form alters perception and inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include post-experimental interviews to probe subjective interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-experimental interviews can reveal how subjects interpret advertising intent and why they may accept illogical favorable inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qualitative follow-ups to complement quantitative measures and to uncover perceptions of advertiser purpose that influence acceptance of statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate applicability of research to practitioners considering organizational constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation and application of academic research must account for firm decision-process structures, timing of commissioned research, and incentive/reward systems that may impede adoption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research is most useful when commissioned in time to be actionable; organizations need disciplined decision processes to act on findings; recognize that sometimes business procedures make implementation difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value academic research for theory, gap identification, and question formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when not directly applicable to a specific campaign, academic research is valuable for advancing scientific knowledge, improving understanding of processes, exposing gaps in knowledge, and helping practitioners ask better questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge research both on direct applicability and on its ability to broaden perspective, suggest new strategies, and serve as prototypes for further tailored studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer life-style variables over only socioeconomic variables for segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Life‑style variables (activities, interests, opinions, values, goals, situational forces) can be more meaningful and useful for segmentation than traditional socioeconomic variables like income and social class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating segments, check whether segments can be reached efficiently by specific media and whether the variables inform appeal selection and persuasive message design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure information-handling and decision-making process variables for purchase behavior studies
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying consumer decision-making, measure information sources used, product exposure prior to purchase, amount of deliberation, number of brands considered, degree of family participation, decision criteria, planned usage, and future purchase plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These variables reveal meaningful differences between life-style groups (e.g., rural vs urban) and help determine appropriate promotion mix and message strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lab findings to challenge and improve media-scheduling models
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental findings on repetition and response shapes should be used to challenge assumed relationships embedded in computer media scheduling models and improve model runs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update media models when empirical laboratory results contradict traditional assumptions (e.g., nonmonotonic curves or thresholds) to obtain better scheduling recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design studies to serve as prototypes and attract further funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Research projects should be constructed so they can serve as prototypes from which similar research can be patterned and so they can attract additional academic or applied support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document methodology and findings clearly; demonstrate broader relevance to encourage follow‑on studies and practical adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the distinctive perception of advertising as purposeful persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: People tend to view advertising as purposeful communication designed to create favorable impressions and may therefore attribute intentions to advertisers that lead to acceptance of favorable but logically invalid inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for this 'tolerance' in designing messages and interpreting consumer responses; test for attribution effects in studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider social value and ethical/social-change implications in advertising research
rubrics_metrics.description: Research should consider advertising's role in reflecting and influencing social climate (e.g., integrated advertising seen as consistent with social change) and the social consequences of ad content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how inclusion and portrayals affect group recognition, social structure perceptions, and potential to reduce prejudice; include normative/ethical analysis where relevant.
